title: Xanthe and the Songbook
premise: Astrid Underhill, a cellist whose career ended in one catastrophic final performance, retreats to her late grandmother's vineyard to catalog an inherited songbook and decide whether to sell. A snowstorm strands her with two estranged rivals from her conservatory days — conductor Elias Vane, the man she once loved, and composer Juno Reyes, who wrote the piece that destroyed Astrid's career — forcing all three to confront the night everything broke. As spring turns toward the vineyard's first harvest, old rivalries soften into something like family, and Astrid must finally say the sentence she has rehearsed for ten years: that she froze because she loved them both and couldn't bear to choose. She performs the songbook's unfinished finale at the harvest festival, keeps the vineyard, and chooses herself first — which is what finally lets love, in present tense, find her.
about_author: Marguerite Ashgrove is the pen name of a former orchestral librarian who spent fifteen years marking bowings for musicians braver than herself. She writes romance in a converted hop barn, accompanied by a deaf terrier named Fermata.

chapters.title: The Inheritance of Small Noises
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. She arrives at the derelict Underhill vineyard with a moving box of rosin, metronomes, and grief, and finds her grandmother's songbook locked in a piano bench. Beat: avoidance dressed as practicality; she tells the solicitor she's only here to appraise and sell.

chapters.title: What the Cellar Keeps
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Cataloging the cellar, she finds a 2009 harvest photo featuring two faces she knows: young Elias Vane and Juno Reyes, laughing beside her grandmother. The songbook's margins contain their handwriting. Beat: dread — the past has been waiting here all along.

chapters.title: Snow Takes the Road
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. An early blizzard strands two cars in the lane: Elias, now a famous conductor, and Juno, now a celebrated composer, both summoned by letters they believed came from Astrid's grandmother. Beat: collision — three people who share one catastrophe trapped under one roof.

chapters.title: Rules of the House
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. He proposes strict neutrality: no talk of the final performance, shared chores, separate wings. Astrid agrees too quickly, which unsettles him more than anger would. Beat: fragile truce established over a generator and bad instant coffee.

chapters.title: Juno Writes at Night
chapters.summary: Juno's POV. Unable to sleep, Juno discovers Astrid practicing scales in the frozen ballroom at 3 a.m. — the first time she's played since the collapse. They don't speak of it. Beat: tenderness disguised as trespass; Juno begins sketching music again.

chapters.title: The Songbook Opens
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. The lock on the piano bench breaks; inside, the songbook reveals her grandmother composed a finale left deliberately unfinished, with instructions: 'to be completed by whoever stays.' Beat: inheritance reframed — not property, but a question.

chapters.title: Two Rivals, One Recipe
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Forced to cook together, Elias and Juno's rivalry resurfaces as comedy — competitive bread-making, sabotage by cinnamon. Astrid laughs for the first time in years and hates how much she likes it. Beat: warmth creeping past the truce.

chapters.title: Interlude: The Night We Don't Discuss
chapters.summary: Triple POV fragments. Each privately recalls the catastrophic final performance: Astrid freezing mid-solo, Elias cutting her off with a downbeat, Juno walking out of the hall. Beat: the reader learns the wound while the characters still refuse to name it.

chapters.title: Pruning Season
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. The trio begins winter pruning; Astrid learns the vines were her grandmother's answer to heartbreak — things cut back so they can bear. She almost tells Elias the truth, then doesn't. Beat: hope undercut by rehearsal of old silence.

chapters.title: Letters, Forged and Otherwise
chapters.summary: Juno's POV. Juno deduces the summoning letters were written by the solicitor on the grandmother's posthumous instruction — a matchmaker from beyond the grave. Confronted, Astrid admits she knew and let them come. Beat: betrayal flickers, then curiosity wins.

chapters.title: Duet in D Minor
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Snowbound intimacy tips over: Elias and Astrid play a two-person arrangement from the songbook and afterward nearly kiss before he retreats, confessing he can't tell where love ends and guilt begins. Beat: desire entangled with debt.

chapters.title: The Review That Never Ran
chapters.summary: Juno's POV. Juno reveals the truth of the final performance: the devastating review was never published; Juno bought every copy to protect Astrid and let her believe the world had condemned her. Beat: the central misunderstanding detonates quietly.

chapters.title: Three Days of Not Speaking
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Astrid goes silent — not angry, but overwhelmed — and works the vines alone. Elias and Juno, rivals no longer, keep the house running for her without being asked. Beat: found family forming in the negative space of her grief.

chapters.title: Bud Break
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Spring arrives; the vines wake. Elias apologizes properly for the downbeat that ended her career, admitting he chose the orchestra over her out of cowardice. Beat: accountability offered, not yet accepted.

chapters.title: What Juno Owes
chapters.summary: Juno's POV. Juno confesses the deeper secret: the piece Astrid froze on was rewritten from a love song Juno wrote about her, and its premiere was meant as a confession Astrid never heard. Beat: love revealed in past tense, waiting to be translated.

chapters.title: The Sentence, Rehearsed
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Alone with the songbook, Astrid finally says it aloud to an empty ballroom: 'I froze because I loved you both and couldn't bear to choose.' Saying it changes nothing and everything. Beat: catharsis — the decade-long rehearsal ends.

chapters.title: Finishing the Finale
chapters.summary: Triple POV. The three compose the songbook's ending together, arguing, laughing, spilling wine on the manuscript. It becomes unmistakably a piece for cello, piano, and two stubborn hearts. Beat: collaboration as reconciliation; the harvest approaches.

chapters.title: First Harvest
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Neighbors, hired hands, and the bemused solicitor arrive for the vineyard's first harvest in a decade. Astrid realizes she isn't appraising the vineyard anymore — she's keeping it. Beat: belonging chosen, not inherited.

chapters.title: The Festival Program
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Elias arranges the harvest festival concert and asks Astrid to perform the finished finale publicly. She refuses twice; Juno refuses to let either of them hide. Beat: rising tension — the stage that broke her waits again.

chapters.title: Climax: The Unfinished Song
chapters.summary: Triple POV converging. At the festival, mid-performance, Astrid freezes exactly as she did ten years ago — and this time Elias holds the tempo open, Juno steps beside her, and the crowd waits without judgment. She plays through. Beat: the catastrophe replayed and rewritten in real time.

chapters.title: Present Tense
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Afterward, under string lights in the cellar, Astrid says the sentence aloud to them both — not as confession but invitation. No one is asked to choose; everyone is asked to stay. Beat: love admitted in present tense, plural and unashamed.

chapters.title: Coda: Whoever Stays
chapters.summary: Epistolary coda, mixed POVs. Letters and margin notes across the following year: Juno's new quartet premiered, Elias conducting from a rebuilt village hall, Astrid teaching cellists in the ballroom. The songbook gains fresh handwriting. Beat: resolution — inheritance fulfilled by staying.
